name: search_papers
description:
Search ONE academic database with ONE search string and save the raw records. Every record is also folded into the corpus table `library/corpus/records.csv` as it arrives, deduplicated on write (by DOI, else by normalised title), and every search is logged with its query string so the query stays findable.

When to use: Literature review, collect stage: the broad first pass, the boolean sweeps, and again when a thin corpus has to be widened. Ideation, screen stage: the quick novelty probe. Approach design: novelty and closely related work.

Parameters & returns:
Parameters:
- `db` (string, required): `crossref`, `arxiv`, `semantic_scholar`, `ieee`, `springer`, `elsevier`, `acm` or `google_scholar`.
- `query` (string, required): ONE search string in THIS database's syntax, e.g. arXiv `abs:"BM25" AND abs:"TF-IDF"`. A typed-out sentence (more than 6 bare content words with no quotes, operators or field prefixes) is rejected everywhere except `crossref`, which matches whole bibliographic phrases and does better with the long form.
- `start_year`, `end_year` (integer, required): publication-year range.
- `max_results` (integer): default 500.
- `purpose` (string, required): a short slug for the SWEEP this query belongs to, shared by every query in it: `map`, `anchors`, `novelty`, `classics`. Not one per query.
- `tag` (string): a short slug for THIS query inside the sweep (`primary`, `c1b`, `rm3`). Required when a sweep runs the same database more than once, or the results overwrite each other.

Returns: a per-database summary (records found; databases that did NOT run, each a coverage gap; databases that ran and matched nothing), then `[corpus: +N new, M already known, T total in library/corpus/records.csv]` and `[saved: records/searches/<purpose>/<db>__<tag>.csv — indexed in records/searches/searches.csv]`. Raw columns: title, authors, year, doi, abstract, venue, url, source_db. `searches.csv` gets one row per search: when, purpose, db, tag, query, start_year, end_year, rows, file.

Example: `{"db": "arxiv", "query": "ti:\"term weighting\" OR ti:\"BM25\"", "start_year": 2015, "end_year": 2026, "purpose": "map", "tag": "primary"}`

Output limit:
Up to `max_results` records per call (ACM stops around 200). Returned text is capped at 8,000 characters, keeping the end; the records are in the saved CSV. Times out after 20 minutes.

Usage steps & restrictions:
1. Read the user's seed papers (`materials/`, brought in with `merge_local_papers`) before writing any query: their vocabulary is the field's, and queries in the field's words come back mostly on topic.
2. One broad `crossref` pass with a plain sentence describing the topic (measured 9–10/10 on topic). Read the titles that come back alongside the seeds'.
3. Then write the strings in the field's words: a primary string (2–3 distinct concepts joined by AND) and one or two OR-expanded ones. Name the subject, not the tool: on arXiv `ti:"term weighting" OR ti:"BM25"` came back ~90% on topic, `ti:"BM25" OR ti:"TF-IDF"` ~20% — a tool name retrieves everyone who used it.
4. Check each string would retrieve the user's own papers. If it would not, it is aimed somewhere else; fix it before it costs a sweep.
5. One call per database × string; never batch databases, so a failure stays attributable. Use each database's syntax: arXiv reads bare words as OR (357,859 hits against 31 for `abs:"BM25" AND abs:"TF-IDF"`), so field prefixes (`abs:`, `ti:`, `all:`) and capitalised `AND`/`OR`/`NOT` are mandatory there.
6. Pick databases by domain, not all of them: CS/ML/NLP → crossref + arxiv (+ semantic_scholar); software engineering → add ieee, acm; security/systems → crossref + arxiv + ieee; journal-heavy or interdisciplinary → crossref + springer, elsevier. Justify every database past five.

- Do not use `google_scholar` unless the user explicitly asked: it needs the optional `scholarly` package, and its scraper can open a browser when blocked. `acm` and `google_scholar` are fragile gap-fill, never load-bearing.
- Keyless `semantic_scholar` cannot be relied on (measured: 0 results, rate-limited through every back-off). Treat it as a bonus unless `S2_API_KEY` is set.
- `ieee`, `springer` and `elsevier` need `IEEE_API_KEY`, `SPRINGER_API_KEY`, `ELSEVIER_API_KEY`; without one they are skipped.
- Novelty probe in Ideation: 2–3 targeted queries per candidate, `purpose: "novelty"`, the candidate id as `tag`. It only catches the obviously already-done; it is not the novelty verdict.
- Dedup is not fuzzy: a subtitle one database dropped leaves two rows for one paper.

On errors:
- `query rejected -- a typed-out sentence, not a search string`: nothing was searched. Rewrite it from papers you have read: fewer than 6 content words or a proper boolean string, with at least one term only your subject uses (a method name, a metric, a system).
- A database listed under "did NOT run" (missing key, blocked scraper, network failure): a coverage gap to report with its fix ("configure IEEE_API_KEY and re-run"), not a silent loss. Each failure is also appended to `records/searches/<purpose>/search_errors.log`.
- `Semantic Scholar never answered (rate-limited after 4 retries)`: the query never ran. It is a gap, not a zero result; set `S2_API_KEY` or report the gap.
- "ran and matched NOTHING" from a database that normally covers the field: suspect the query's syntax before accepting the zero.

Effect: Writes local files.

name: backfill_abstracts
description:
Look up the abstracts missing from the corpus table by DOI (an OpenAlex record fetch, not a search) and write them back into `library/corpus/records.csv`. Empty venue and year are filled from the same record.

When to use: Literature review, collect stage: after the searches, before the first screening pass.

Parameters & returns:
Parameters:
- `corpus_csv` (string): the corpus table; default `library/corpus/records.csv`.

Returns: how many records lack a usable abstract (under 80 characters counts as missing) and how many of those carry a DOI, then checked / missing / filled / still missing.

Example: `{"corpus_csv": "library/corpus/records.csv"}`

Output limit:
Looks up 50 DOIs per request. Returned text is capped at 8,000 characters, keeping the end. Times out after 15 minutes.

Usage steps & restrictions:
Run it BEFORE screening. Crossref returns DOI registration metadata and publishers often register no abstract: on one sweep 27% of crossref records had one against 100% of arXiv's, and this lookup recovered 13 of 18. A paper judged on its title alone is kept to be safe, so every missing abstract becomes a full-text download one sentence would have avoided. Records with no DOI, or that the lookup does not know, keep their empty abstract and are reported, not dropped.

On errors:
- `no corpus at <path>`: nothing has been searched yet, or the path is wrong. Run `search_papers` first.
- `lookup failed for N dois`: a network failure on that batch; those abstracts stay empty. Re-run: rows already filled are not looked up again.

Effect: Writes local files.

name: snowball_papers
description:
Expand the SCREENED included set along its citations — the papers they cite (backward), the papers citing them (forward), or both — to find what the keyword search missed. Candidates come back deduplicated against what you already have, ranked by `co_citation_count` (how many included papers led to each), and are folded into `library/corpus/records.csv`, deduplicated on write, so screening sees one list.

When to use: Literature review, collect stage, phase 3: after the first screening and `prisma_report`, repeated round by round.

Parameters & returns:
Parameters:
- `mode` (string, required): `backward`, `forward` or `both`.
- `input_csv` (string, required in practice): the included set to expand from, normally `library/corpus/CORPUS_PAPERS.csv`.
- `existing_corpus_csv` (string): what you already have, so candidates come back deduped — `library/corpus/records.csv`.
- `output_dir` (string): where candidates land, e.g. `library/snowball`.
- `start_year`, `end_year` (integer): default 2014 and 2025 — set them explicitly. They bound forward hops only; backward hops ignore them, because the classics a field stands on are old by definition.

Returns: the run log (per input paper: how it resolved, how many new references or citations), skipped rows, `Total unique new candidates: N (M reached from 2+ input papers)`, a summary, and `[corpus: +N new from snowballing, M already known]`. Writes `backward_candidates.csv` and `forward_candidates.csv` (plus `snowball_candidates.csv` for `both`), sorted by `co_citation_count`, with `source_papers`.

Example: `{"mode": "both", "input_csv": "library/corpus/CORPUS_PAPERS.csv", "existing_corpus_csv": "library/corpus/records.csv", "output_dir": "library/snowball", "start_year": 2015, "end_year": 2026}`

Output limit:
Up to 500 references or citations per input paper. Many small API calls: about 1.5 s apart without `S2_API_KEY`, 0.3 s with it. Returned text is capped at 8,000 characters, keeping the end — the per-paper log is long, so the summary is at the end. Times out after 30 minutes.

Usage steps & restrictions:
- Input rows resolve by arXiv id (exact), then DOI, then title search.
- `co_citation_count` is the signal a keyword search cannot give: a paper reached from four included papers is load-bearing even if it contains none of your query terms.
- New candidates are screened exactly like search results (`paper-screener` batches); then re-run `prisma_report`.
- Then snowball again from the corpus you now have. Stop when a full round adds nothing new that survives screening, and say which round went dry (two rounds is common, one is possible, four happens in a field that cites sideways).
- Each round should be less central than the last (`co_citation_count` falling). A round as strongly co-cited as the first means the search missed a whole sub-direction: say so.
- If a round goes dry while the corpus is still thin, do not snowball again: go back to `search_papers` and widen (vocabulary from the titles you already have, a database that returned nothing). Snowballing only reaches papers connected to the ones you have.
- Report the yield — how many included papers it added over the search measures how blind the search was — and the unresolved rows.

On errors:
- `No S2_API_KEY set`: strict rate limits; rows may fail to resolve.
- `Semantic Scholar refused N calls in a row … continuing on the OpenAlex fallback`: OpenAlex has no reference lists for arXiv preprints (measured 0/105), so report this expansion as degraded, not as coverage.
- `Skipped k/n papers (no S2 OR OpenAlex match)`: each skip weakens the co-citation signal; report the number.
- A missing `input_csv` fails the call: run `prisma_report` first, which writes `CORPUS_PAPERS.csv`.

Effect: Writes local files.

name: download_papers
description:
Fetch a PDF for each paper through the open-access cascade: direct URL, arXiv, Unpaywall (`UNPAYWALL_EMAIL`), DOI resolve, publisher OA pages. Sci-Hub is not in the cascade. A paper it cannot get becomes a placeholder `.txt` file listed in `download_report.md` — never a silent drop.

When to use: Literature review, collect stage, before the full-text screening pass; again for late arrivals, and whenever a paper you will lean on is not on disk.

Parameters & returns:
Parameters:
- `input_csv` (string, required): `sought` — the usual case — collects every paper the abstract pass marked `sought`, joins it to the corpus metadata itself, and fetches those. Or a project-relative CSV path to fetch exactly what it names (an id column `paper_id`, `key` or `record_id`, plus `title`, `doi`, `url`).
- `output_dir` (string, required): where the PDFs go, `library/corpus/papers`.
- `delay` (number): seconds between requests, default 2.0.

Returns: with `sought`, `Collected N sought paper(s) into library/corpus/sought.csv`; per paper `OK <method>` or `FAILED (<strategies tried>) -> placeholder created`; a summary (total, success %, failed, report path); and `X paper(s) have a PDF and stay in library/corpus/sought.csv (with a pdf column); Y could not be fetched and now carry a not_retrieved decision`.

Example: `{"input_csv": "sought", "output_dir": "library/corpus/papers"}`

Output limit:
One request every `delay` seconds. Returned text is capped at 8,000 characters, keeping the end; the full list is in `download_report.md`. Times out after 60 minutes.

Usage steps & restrictions:
1. Check the size of the `sought` set first. A full-text set is normally in the low hundreds at most; one approaching the size of the corpus means the abstract pass sorted rather than filtered. Re-screen `sought` against the depth rule instead — half an hour of abstracts beats five hours of PDFs.
2. Pass `sought`; never build that list yourself.
3. Afterwards `library/corpus/sought.csv` holds only the papers it fetched, each with its `pdf` path. That file is the list for the full-text `paper-screener` batch (one paper per helper).

- Unfetched papers get their decision file set to `not_retrieved` (stage `retrieval`, the screening `why` kept). `not_retrieved` is a number the funnel reports, never a silent exclusion: list those papers in your step report. If the user later puts one of these PDFs into `materials/`, judge that paper on its full text then.
- Safe to re-run: PDFs already on disk are skipped.

On errors:
- `No papers are marked sought (or the corpus table is missing)`: nothing to fetch. The abstract pass has produced no `sought` decisions, or `library/corpus/records.csv` is missing.
- `N sought id(s) had no row in the corpus table`: those could not be fetched; report them.
- Timeout: the PDFs fetched so far are on disk; re-run and they are skipped.

Effect: Writes local files.

name: merge_local_papers
description:
Merge the user's own PDFs into the corpus: extract each PDF's metadata (pymupdf + Semantic Scholar lookup), match it against the included set (exact DOI, then fuzzy title), tag every row `source = slr / local / slr+local`, and write `CORPUS_PAPERS.csv`, `LOCAL_MERGE_LOG.csv` and `CORPUS_SUMMARY.md` into `corpus_dir`, copying the PDFs into its `papers/`.

When to use: Literature review, collect stage: phase 1 (the seed papers in `materials/`, before any query), and again for PDFs the user adds later.

Parameters & returns:
Parameters:
- `local_dir` (string, required): the folder of user PDFs, `materials` (top level only).
- `slr_csv` (string, required): the included papers, `library/corpus/CORPUS_PAPERS.csv` (may not exist yet).
- `corpus_dir` (string, required): `library/corpus`.
- `slr_papers_dir` (string): already-downloaded PDFs, default `library/corpus/papers`.
- `title_threshold` (number): fuzzy title match, default 0.85.

Returns: local PDFs scanned, newly added, duplicates skipped, conflicts flagged, and the final corpus count (SLR | local | overlap). `LOCAL_MERGE_LOG.csv` has one row per PDF: filename, paper_id, title, year, status (`added`, `duplicate`, `conflict_flagged`), duplicate_of, notes.

Example: `{"local_dir": "materials", "slr_csv": "library/corpus/CORPUS_PAPERS.csv", "corpus_dir": "library/corpus"}`

Output limit:
Returned text is capped at 8,000 characters, keeping the end. Times out after 30 minutes.

Usage steps & restrictions:
- Read the seeds' titles, abstracts and keywords before writing a single query, and keep their paper ids: they are the vocabulary for your queries and the `seed_ids` for `check_screening`. If `materials/` is empty, say so — you are working without that baseline.
- Seeds are screened like every other paper: `prisma_report` rebuilds `CORPUS_PAPERS.csv` from the decision files, so a paper counts in the corpus only once it has a decision.
- `conflict` rows (similar title, different DOI) are not yours to settle by guessing: do not merge or drop them; list them in your step report for the user.

On errors:
- `[SKIP] no local papers directory at <dir>`: nothing was merged; say that you are working without seed papers.
- A PDF whose metadata cannot be extracted is still added under its filename; check its row in `LOCAL_MERGE_LOG.csv`.

Effect: Writes local files.

name: parse_pdfs
description:
Batch-parse PDFs into one structured JSON per paper — title, authors, abstract, `paper_text`, `sections`, `references` — using the engine cascade opendataloader-pdf → pymupdf → pdfminer. Metadata from `meta_csv` takes priority over what the parser finds.

When to use: Literature review: when many papers need their text in machine-usable form (the digest stage, and `cites` edges for `build_kg`).

Parameters & returns:
Parameters:
- `pdf_dir` (string, required): `library/corpus/papers`.
- `out_dir` (string, required): `library/paper_cards/parsed`.
- `meta_csv` (string): `library/corpus/CORPUS_PAPERS.csv`, the metadata priority source.
- `log_csv` (string): default `<out_dir>/PARSE_LOG.csv`.

Returns: one line per PDF (`OK` or `FAILED — <reason>`) and `Parsing complete: X/Y succeeded`. Each card is `<out_dir>/<pdf file stem>.json` with paper_id, title, authors, year, venue, url, local_path, abstract, paper_text, sections, references, parse_engine, parse_status.

Example: `{"pdf_dir": "library/corpus/papers", "out_dir": "library/paper_cards/parsed", "meta_csv": "library/corpus/CORPUS_PAPERS.csv"}`

Output limit:
Returned text is capped at 8,000 characters, keeping the end; per-paper status is in `PARSE_LOG.csv`. Every run re-parses every PDF in `pdf_dir`. Times out after 30 minutes.

Usage steps & restrictions:
- It is for batches. To judge one paper, open the PDF itself: measured on a retrieval paper, the text parser dropped a nested results table and the verdict flipped.
- Scanned or encrypted PDFs land as `failed` in `PARSE_LOG.csv` without stopping the run. A failed paper is INVISIBLE to every later phase: count the failures and report them as a degradation, with the number.

On errors:
- `[WARN] No PDF files found in <dir>`: nothing downloaded yet, or the wrong folder. Run `download_papers` first.
- A `pdf_dir` that does not exist fails the call.

Effect: Writes local files.

name: check_screening
description:
Count the screening decisions on disk and report what is unfinished: papers still `sought` (full text never fetched), corpus records with no decision file at all, files that fail the decision schema, unreadable files, and — given the seed ids — whether the user's own papers survived the criteria. It COUNTS files; it judges nothing and changes nothing.

When to use: Literature review, collect stage: after every `paper-screener` batch, and before you call screening done.

Parameters & returns:
Parameters:
- `screen_dir` (string): the decision files; default `library/screening/papers`.
- `corpus_csv` (string): the corpus table; default `library/corpus/records.csv`.
- `seed_ids` (array of strings): the user's own papers, as paper ids.

Returns one fact per line: `N records · M decided · excluded=… · sought=… · included=…`, then whichever apply — `STILL SOUGHT (n)`, `NO DECISION FILE (n)`, `UNRECOGNISED OUTCOME (n)`, `INVALID (n)` (fails the schema: outcome, stage, why, reason_code), `UNREADABLE (n)`, `seeds: k/n survived — EXCLUDED: …` — or `Every record in the corpus has a settled decision.`

A valid decision file has `paper_id`; `outcome` ∈ excluded, sought, not_retrieved, included, uncertain; `stage` ∈ screening, retrieval, eligibility; a non-empty `why`; and a `reason_code` when excluded or not_retrieved.

Example: `{"seed_ids": ["arxiv:2305.14314", "doi:10.1145/3626772.3657895"]}`

Output limit:
Each list shows up to 12 ids, then `… (+N more)`.

Usage steps & restrictions:
- Nothing else checks what the `paper-screener` helpers wrote; this does.
- Give exactly the NO DECISION FILE, INVALID and UNREADABLE ids to a new `paper-screener` batch with the same brief. A count that stops moving across two passes is a real problem to look at, not a number to keep re-sending.
- Screening is done when this reports `sought=0` — not when the batch looks finished. If you stop early, stop on the record: how many are unresolved, why you stopped, and what it costs the conclusion. (Seen live: a crashed downloader left 43 papers `sought`, 13 of them plain arXiv PDFs, and the phase was reported complete.)
- A seed the criteria excluded is a message about the criteria: read which criterion cut it before accepting the exclusion.

On errors:
- `Nothing to check: no decisions … and no records …`: search and screen first.
- `<file>: no id column (looked for key/paper_id/record_id) — the 'never judged' count below is NOT trustworthy`: `corpus_csv` points at the wrong table; pass `library/corpus/records.csv`.

Effect: Read-only.

name: prisma_report
description:
Recompute the screening funnel from `library/screening/papers/*.json` and write two derived files: `library/screening/prisma.md` (the PRISMA 2020 funnel) and `library/corpus/CORPUS_PAPERS.csv` (the included papers joined to the metadata they were retrieved with — the ONE corpus table everything downstream reads).

When to use: Literature review, collect stage: after the full-text pass, and again after ANY screening change (a snowball round, a re-screen, a late PDF).

Parameters & returns:
Parameters:
- `screen_dir` (string): default `library/screening/papers`.
- `output` (string): default `library/screening/prisma.md`.
- `corpus_csv` (string): `library/corpus/records.csv` — gives the records-identified count and the metadata joined onto included papers. Always pass it.
- `corpus_out` (string): default `library/corpus/CORPUS_PAPERS.csv`.

Returns: `N decisions: excluded=…, sought=…, not_retrieved=…, included=…, uncertain=…`, a note if any are still `sought`, a warning if files were unreadable, and `Wrote <output> and <corpus_out> (n papers)`.

Example: `{"corpus_csv": "library/corpus/records.csv"}`

Output limit:
Returned text is capped at 8,000 characters, keeping the end. Times out after 2 minutes.

Usage steps & restrictions:
- Every count comes from the decision files. Re-run it instead of writing numbers down: a figure typed into prose goes stale the moment a paper moves, and nothing catches it.
- Never edit `prisma.md` or `CORPUS_PAPERS.csv` by hand; both are rewritten on every run, so they can never disagree with the decisions. Included and `uncertain` papers go into `CORPUS_PAPERS.csv`.

On errors:
- `No screening directory at <dir>`: nothing has been screened yet.
- `WARNING: N unreadable file(s) are NOT counted`: they are listed in `prisma.md` as uncounted; have those papers re-judged.

Effect: Writes local files.

name: check_extractions
description:
The deterministic commit step for the per-paper extractions: read every decision file in `library/screening/papers/` that carries an extraction (written by the `paper-screener` that included the paper), check it against the paper's card, normalise it to the schema, flag missing, invalid and empty extractions, and assemble the valid ones into `structured_papers.jsonl` for `build_kg`. Screening keys are ignored. No LLM.

When to use: Literature review, digest stage: after screening is settled, before `build_kg`.

Parameters & returns:
Parameters:
- `parsed_dir` (string, required): parsed cards, `library/paper_cards/parsed`. Optional in effect: papers included on their abstract have no card and are covered from their decision file.
- `structured_dir` (string, required): where the extractions are, `library/screening/papers`.
- `out_jsonl` (string, required): `library/knowledge_graph/structured_papers.jsonl`.
- `report_json` (string): default beside `out_jsonl` (`structured_papers.report.json`).

Returns: a JSON report — `papers_total`, `valid`, `missing` (ids with no extraction found), `invalid` (`{paper_id, error}`), `empty_extraction` (ids with no problems and no methods), `out` — also written to `report_json`.

Example: `{"parsed_dir": "library/paper_cards/parsed", "structured_dir": "library/screening/papers", "out_jsonl": "library/knowledge_graph/structured_papers.jsonl"}`

Output limit:
Error text per invalid paper is cut at 300 characters. Times out after 10 minutes.

Usage steps & restrictions:
- Do not re-extract. The extraction was written by the helper that had the full text open; a second pass that cannot see the first one's work is the waste this design removed.
- Every `included` paper should have extraction keys (`summary`, `methods`, …). `not_retrieved` papers have none by definition — a reported gap, not a failure.
- Give each flagged id back to a `paper-screener` for a full-text judgement (one paper per helper), then re-run this until the report is clean or the residue is explained.

On errors:
- `missing`: an included paper with no extraction — a bug; have it re-judged on its full text.
- `invalid`: the file does not normalise to the schema (the error says why); have it re-extracted.
- `empty_extraction`: no problems and no methods, so it would add nothing to the graph; have it re-extracted.
- A paper whose PDF never parsed has nothing to extract; it is already counted as a parse failure.

Effect: Writes local files.

name: search_datasets
description:
Search for candidate public datasets and append them to a candidates CSV. Two keyless sources: `hf` (HuggingFace Hub datasets — name, description, size hint, license, downloads) and `openalex` (papers that introduce datasets or benchmarks; many benchmarks exist only as a paper artifact). Returns CANDIDATES ONLY: whether any of them can carry your claim is your judgment.

When to use: Dataset, search stage: once per phrasing, including the mismatch probes.

Parameters & returns:
Parameters:
- `query` (string, required): one phrasing. HF matches names and tags near-literally — short, name-like queries work (`tool use`, `multi-hop QA`); a four-word natural phrase returns nothing. OpenAlex takes longer descriptive phrases.
- `output_csv` (string, required): `dataset/candidates.csv`.
- `source` (string): `hf`, `openalex` or `both` (default).
- `limit` (integer): per source, default 25.
- `min_downloads` (integer): HF only, drop candidates below this download count (default 0).

Returns: `N candidates appended → dataset/candidates.csv (total T)`. Columns: candidate_id (`D001`, … continuing across calls), source, name, url, description, size_hint, popularity, license, tags.

Example: `{"query": "multi-hop QA", "output_csv": "dataset/candidates.csv", "source": "hf"}`

Output limit:
Descriptions cut at 600 characters. Times out after 10 minutes.

Usage steps & restrictions:
- One call per phrasing; the CSV appends. One phrasing finds one vocabulary, and three phrasings in your own words are one phrasing: vary the words the community would use.
- Phrase per source. Running the same long phrase on both sources and concluding "no data exists" is a search failure, not a finding.
- Search the field's standard datasets by name. If a standard set does not show up in a generic search, search it directly rather than concluding it is absent.
- Run the disqualifying (mismatch) queries too, so a near-miss reaches the review with its evidence attached.
- Record what you could not search (sources needing a key, gated datasets, anything behind a login) as a coverage limit.

On errors:
- `[hf] search failed` / `[openalex] search failed`: that source returned nothing because the request failed, not because nothing exists. Re-run it.
- `Error: source must be hf, openalex or both`.

Effect: Writes local files.

name: validate_dataset
description:
Mechanically check a datapoint JSONL and write the clean copy: each line parses as a JSON object, required fields are present and non-empty, exact duplicates are removed, and optionally the value distribution of one field is reported. The report lists what it checked AND what it deliberately did not.

When to use: Dataset, synthesize stage: after the `datapoint-generator` helpers have written the raw datapoints.

Parameters & returns:
Parameters:
- `input_jsonl` (string, required): raw datapoints, e.g. `dataset/synthetic/datapoints.raw.jsonl`.
- `output_jsonl` (string, required): clean output, e.g. `dataset/synthetic/datapoints.jsonl`.
- `report_json` (string): default beside `output_jsonl` (`datapoints.report.json`).
- `require` (string): comma-separated required field names.
- `group_by` (string): field to report a value distribution for (the stratum or variant label).

Returns: the report as JSON — `lines_in`, `valid`, `unparsable`, `missing_fields` and `duplicates` (each a count and a sample), `required_fields`, `distribution` (distinct values and the most common), `checks_performed`, `checks_NOT_performed` (whether the data operationalises the claim, whether the distribution matches the intended topology, label correctness, contamination against the evaluated model).

Example: `{"input_jsonl": "dataset/synthetic/datapoints.raw.jsonl", "output_jsonl": "dataset/synthetic/datapoints.jsonl", "require": "id,input,variant", "group_by": "variant"}`

Output limit:
Up to 5 sample lines per problem type and the 12 most common values. Returned text is capped at 8,000 characters, keeping the end. Times out after 5 minutes.

Usage steps & restrictions:
- A clean report is a floor, not a verdict. Read the rows yourself for whether the data operationalises the claim and whether the distribution is right.
- Check the contamination controls explicitly: no copied benchmark items, and the generator must not also be the judge in the later experiment (if it would be, say so now — it changes the experiment design).
- Rows that fail a check are dropped from the output, not repaired. `output_jsonl` is overwritten on every run.

On errors:
`lines_in: 0`: the input path is wrong or the file is empty — and an empty output file has been written. Fix the path and re-run.

Effect: Writes local files.

name: run_code
description:
Run project code and get its output — the one execution channel. `entry` is a project-relative Python file run with the platform interpreter, with the project root as working directory, so relative paths inside it resolve against the root. With `pytest: true`, run the test suite under `entry` (a directory) instead.

When to use: Implementation (every component, the tests, the pilot) and Evaluation (every run, after `check_script`); Dataset when generating data with code.

Parameters & returns:
Parameters:
- `entry` (string, required): a `.py` file, or a directory when `pytest` is true.
- `args` (array of strings): arguments passed to the script.
- `pytest` (boolean): run `pytest -q` over `entry` instead of executing it.
- `timeout_sec` (integer): default 600, max 3600.

Returns: `exit=<code>` followed by the tail of the combined stdout and stderr.

Example: `{"entry": "experiments/runs/003/run.py", "args": ["--seed", "42", "--slice", "toy"], "timeout_sec": 900}`

Output limit:
Output capped at 8,000 characters, keeping the end (`[... N chars truncated ...]`). Runs at most 3,600 seconds.

Usage steps & restrictions:
- There is no shell: no command strings, no other executables. Write the code to a file and run that.
- A component you have not executed does not work. Build one component, run it (a tiny driver, an import check or a unit test), fix it before the next one builds on it; `pytest: true` over `code/tests/`.
- Toy first, always: run the pilot on the smallest slice that exercises the whole path and check it writes every metric key in the contract. A full run that dies at 80% teaches nothing ten items would not have shown in two minutes.
- In Evaluation, every runner passes `check_script` first, and every run — failed ones too — goes into `record_result`.
- If anything is random, run it twice with the same seed and expect the same result.
- It runs with the agent's own privileges and environment (there is no OS sandbox on a development machine), so it is exactly as safe as the code you wrote.

On errors:
- A non-zero exit is information, not a failure of the tool: read the traceback, fix the code, re-run. A run that cannot complete is recorded too (`status: failed`).
- `Error: <entry> timed out after Ns`: partial work may have been written — check the output files.
- `Error: '<path>' is outside the workspace`, `Error: no such path`, `Error: <path> is a directory — pass a .py file, or set pytest: true`: fix the argument; nothing ran.

Effect: Writes local files.

name: map_codebase
description:
Build a static map of a Python codebase without reading the source into your context: modules with their top-level functions and classes (with signatures), entry points (files with a `__main__` guard), CLI options per file (argparse/click), and the files that write structured results. Pure AST, no LLM.

When to use: Evaluation, map stage: before planning runs against code — especially code you did not write.

Parameters & returns:
Parameters:
- `root` (string, required): the code folder, e.g. `code`.
- `output_json` (string, required): where to write the full map, e.g. `experiments/code_map.json`.

Returns: a JSON summary (`files_scanned`, `entry_points`, `result_writers`) and `full map → <path>`. The full map also holds `config_options`, `modules` and `unparsable`.

Example: `{"root": "code", "output_json": "experiments/code_map.json"}`

Output limit:
Scans at most 400 files (skipping .git, __pycache__, virtualenvs, node_modules); module docstrings cut at 200 characters; only the summary is returned, the rest is in `output_json`. Times out after 5 minutes.

Usage steps & restrictions:
- Read the map, not the source; that is what the tool is for.
- For every planned run, answer from the map: does the entry point exist, can the thing the comparison varies be configured, does it write the metrics the decision rule needs?
- It is static: whether an entry point actually produces those metrics is answered by RUNNING it (`run_code`).
- Something the plan needs and the code lacks: fix it here if small (edit, then `run_code` to confirm), or send it back to Implementation if substantial.

On errors:
`Error: no such directory: <root>`: wrong folder; nothing was written.

Effect: Writes local files.

name: check_script
description:
Check an experiment runner statically against the integrity contract BEFORE you run it. FAILS on: no `main()` or `main()` never called under a `__main__` guard; no structured output (JSON or CSV); a silent `except: pass` (a failed run that looks successful); metrics assembled from literal constants (a hard-coded result). WARNS on: randomness imported but nothing seeded; subprocess without stderr handling; no CLI surface.

When to use: Evaluation, run stage: on every generated or edited runner, before `run_code`.

Parameters & returns:
Parameters:
- `script` (string, required): the runner, e.g. `experiments/runs/003/run.py`.

Returns: JSON `{script, pass, failures: [...], warnings: [...]}`.

Example: `{"script": "experiments/runs/003/run.py"}`

Output limit:
Times out after 2 minutes.

Usage steps & restrictions:
- FAILs are not style notes: these are the failures that produce plausible numbers from nothing. Fix and re-check before running; a failing script is not run as-is.
- WARNs mean run it, but know it: an unseeded run is not reproducible; a child process that dies quietly takes its explanation with it; no CLI surface is fine for a fixed pilot and a smell for a comparison that must vary exactly one thing.

On errors:
`no such script: <path>` or `syntax error: …` come back as failures in the JSON (`pass: false`). Fix the path or the code and re-check.

Effect: Read-only.

name: record_result
description:
Append measured results to the metrics ledger `experiments/metrics.csv` — the entry point every later reader uses. Every row carries the claim it measures (`claim_id`) and the run that produced it (`run_id`); the tool refuses rows without them, and refuses `status: ok` with an empty result, because an untraceable or empty number is not evidence.

When to use: Evaluation, run stage: after every run, failed ones included.

Parameters & returns:
Parameters:
- `metrics_csv` (string, required): `experiments/metrics.csv`.
- `claim_id` (string, required): the Claims list entry this measures (its id in `claims.md`, e.g. `F12`).
- `run_id` (string, required): the run that produced it, e.g. `003`.
- `system` (string, required): `method`, `baseline`, or a named system.
- `config` (string): config label, default `default`.
- `metric` (string) + `value` (string): one metric, its key spelled exactly as the spec spells it.
- `from_json` (string): instead of metric/value, a results file; every numeric field becomes one row (nested keys joined with `.`).
- `n` (string): sample size behind the value.
- `status` (string): `ok` (default), `partial` or `failed`.
- `source` (string): pointer to the raw output (defaults to `from_json`).
- `note` (string).

Returns: `recorded k row(s) → experiments/metrics.csv (claim F12 · run 003 · method)`, or `REFUSED: <reason>` with nothing written. Columns: recorded_at, claim_id, run_id, system, config, metric, value, n, status, source, note.

Example: `{"metrics_csv": "experiments/metrics.csv", "claim_id": "F12", "run_id": "003", "system": "method", "config": "default", "from_json": "experiments/runs/003/results.json", "n": "50"}`

Output limit:
Times out after 2 minutes.

Usage steps & restrictions:
- Append-only: rows are never edited.
- Record failed runs too (`status: failed`): a run that could not complete is information about the method, not an absence of information.
- An "ok" row with no value silently becomes a zero in someone's mean; that is why the refusal exists.

On errors:
`REFUSED` means nothing was written:
- `claim_id and run_id are both required`: find the Claims list entry and the run.
- `status=ok with an empty value` / `status=ok but the results file contains no numeric metric`: record it as `failed` or `partial`, or supply the number.
- `no such results file`: fix the `from_json` path.
- `pass --metric/--value or --from-json`, or an invalid `status`: fix the arguments.

Effect: Writes local files.

name: export_citations
description:
Write a BibTeX file from the project corpus for the papers actually used: pass the documents that cite them and only the entries those documents mention are exported (or `all: true` for the whole corpus). A paper counts as mentioned by its title (first 60 characters), its short system name, its DOI, its arXiv id, or `paper <id>`. Entries with neither a DOI nor an arXiv id are emitted marked `% UNVERIFIED` — identifiers are never invented to make an entry look complete.

When to use: Deliver, package stage.

Parameters & returns:
Parameters:
- `corpus_csv` (string, required): `library/corpus/CORPUS_PAPERS.csv`.
- `output_bib` (string, required): e.g. `deliverables/references.bib`.
- `used` (array of strings): project-relative documents whose mentions select the entries — the handoff, the landscape report, `claims.md`.
- `all` (boolean): export every corpus row.

Returns: `N entries → <output_bib> (U UNVERIFIED)`, with a note when nothing was selected.

Example: `{"corpus_csv": "library/corpus/CORPUS_PAPERS.csv", "used": ["deliverables/handoff.md", "library/landscape/landscape_report.md", "claims.md"], "output_bib": "deliverables/references.bib"}`

Output limit:
Times out after 5 minutes.

Usage steps & restrictions:
- Check the output: list every `% UNVERIFIED` entry in the handoff so the writer knows to verify it, and never add an identifier to make the file look clean.
- `output_bib` is rewritten on every run; fix a wrong entry in the corpus and re-export rather than editing the file.

On errors:
- `Error: no such corpus`: wrong `corpus_csv`; run `prisma_report` if `CORPUS_PAPERS.csv` does not exist yet.
- `[warn] no such document: <path>`: that document was not searched for mentions; fix the path, or its citations are missing from the file.
- `nothing was selected`: neither `used` nor `all` was given.

Effect: Writes local files.

name: web_search
description:
Search the web. Returns the title, URL and extracted text of the best matches. Use it to find recent or external information.

When to use: Alignment: light checks that change the project definition (does relevant literature appear to exist, does a named dataset or benchmark exist, is a resource accessible, is a central factual assumption true). Literature review, landscape stage: recent surveys and reviews the corpus missed.

Parameters & returns:
Parameters:
- `query` (string, required): a short search query.
- `max_results` (integer): 1–10, default 5.
- `domains` (array of strings): only search these domains, e.g. `["arxiv.org"]`.

Returns: numbered results, each with its title, URL and extracted text; or `No web results for: <query>`.

Example: `{"query": "survey of LLM-based research agents 2026", "max_results": 5}`

Output limit:
At most 10 results; each result's text cut at 1,500 characters and the whole answer at 12,000 (`(k more results left out to keep this short.)`); queries longer than 400 characters are cut. Times out after 30 seconds.

Usage steps & restrictions:
During Alignment keep it light: stop when you have enough to make the alignment decision, and do not begin the literature review.

On errors:
- `Web search unavailable — add a Tavily key in Settings`: search is not configured; carry on without it and note the gap.
- `Tavily rejected the key` / `Tavily search limit reached`: the key or quota needs the user; note the gap.
- `timed out; try again or search more narrowly` / `could not reach …; try again later`: transient; retry once, narrower.

Effect: Sends externally.

name: ask_user
description:
Ask the user a question and WAIT for their answer.

When to use: At the user decision points (see Decision rights), and whenever a decision is genuinely theirs: a trade-off you cannot settle from the project files, a missing input only they can supply, a direction that would waste work if guessed wrong.

Parameters & returns:
Parameters:
- `question` (string, required): the whole question, self-contained. It may reach them by email with none of the interface around it; they cannot see your context.
- `options` (array): for a closed decision, the choices, each `{label, description}` — the label is what they click, the description says what it means and what it costs. Omit for an open question.
- `context` (string): what you found that raised the question — the evidence, briefly. Shown with it.

Returns: `The user answered: <answer>`.

Example: `{"question": "No public dataset tests multi-turn tool selection under execution feedback. Switch to synthetic data?", "options": [{"label": "Synthetic", "description": "Generate ~500 controlled dialogues; the result holds for the synthetic setting only."}, {"label": "Closest public set", "description": "Use the nearest single-turn set; it cannot test the multi-turn claim."}], "context": "Searched HF and OpenAlex with 9 phrasings; the 3 near-misses are single-turn only (dataset/review.md)."}`

Usage steps & restrictions:
- It blocks until they answer, so ask only when the answer changes what you do next, and say what you will get on with meanwhile if there is something useful.
- Do not ask what you can find out or infer, and do not hand the user routine research decisions: which databases to search, which query to try first, how to organise exploration, an obvious methodological convention, whether a claim can be checked independently — decide those yourself.
- Ask everything that needs asking in one go; later questions ask only what the answers raised.

On errors:
`No answer came back. Nobody has answered yet — do not read that as agreement.`: do not proceed as if approved. Go on with work that does not depend on the answer, or stop and wait.

Effect: Read-only.

name: request_folder_access
description:
Request read-only access to an existing directory on the user's machine, outside the app's own data directory and app bundle, explaining why the project needs it. The user must Allow or Deny. An Allow takes effect from your NEXT session, not the one currently running.

When to use: When the project needs files that sit in a folder outside the project (the user's own code, data or papers) and have not been put in `materials/`.

Parameters & returns:
Parameters:
- `path` (string, required): an absolute path to an existing directory.
- `reason` (string, required): why this project needs to read it.

Returns: `Folder access allowed for <path>. It is read-only and takes effect for your next session.`, `Folder access denied for <path>.`, or the user's own message.

Example: `{"path": "/Users/me/projects/retrieval-baselines", "reason": "The user's baseline implementation; the evaluation reuses its BM25 runner."}`

Usage steps & restrictions:
Access is read-only and starts next session: do not try to read the folder in this one. Plan the work that needs it for later.

On errors:
- `Folder access denied`: work without it; the files can still come in through `materials/`.
- `folder access is not available in this mode`: the tool works only in desktop isolation mode; the files have to come in through `materials/`.

Effect: Read-only.

name: update_plan
description:
View and update this project's plan and to-dos.

When to use: When you start an item, finish an item, get stuck, or need to add a to-do.

Parameters & returns:
Parameters:
- `action`: `list` to view, `add` to add an item, `update` to change an item.
- `step`: which of the seven steps it belongs to.
- `item`: when adding, the content of the to-do; when updating, its number.
- `status`: to do, in progress, done, dropped, blocked.
- `note`: the reason for dropping, or what you're waiting on when blocked.

Returns: the updated plan and the to-dos for the current step.

Effect: Writes local files.
